title: AI & ML Foundations
desc: The mathematical engine under everything else — concept-first so the math always serves a purpose you can see.

units.title: The Learning Problem
units.meta: Data, model, loss — the three components

watch.title: CS229 Lecture 1 — Introduction (Andrew Ng)
watch.focus: First 40 min. Supervised learning definition, notation (x,y,h,J), three ML components: data, model, loss.

concept.title: Learning = finding the function that fits
concept.body: Every ML problem: Data {(x⁽ⁱ⁾,y⁽ⁱ⁾)}, Model h_θ(x), Loss J(θ). Learning = find θ that minimizes J(θ). Everything in ML is a variation of this.
concept.analogy: Learning is calibrating a measuring instrument. Ground truth measurements (data), adjustable formula (model), error score (loss). Adjust parameters to minimize score.
concept.visual:
Data: {(x⁽¹⁾,y⁽¹⁾),...,(x⁽ⁿ⁾,y⁽ⁿ⁾)}
Model: h_θ(x) — parameterized function
Loss: J(θ) = (1/n)·Σ L(h_θ(xⁱ), yⁱ)
Goal: θ* = argmin_θ J(θ)

challenge.q: Training a chest X-ray classifier outputting probability of pneumonia. Most appropriate loss?

opts.t: MSE — minimizes difference between predicted and true probability
Binary cross-entropy — measures how well predicted probability explains the true binary label
Hinge loss — standard for binary classification
L1 loss — robust to outliers in medical data

challenge.hint: Output is probability (0–1). True label is binary (0 or 1). Which loss is designed for this?
challenge.exp: Binary cross-entropy: L = -[y·log(p)+(1-y)·log(1-p)]. Derived from maximum likelihood estimation for Bernoulli outcomes. Directly connects to your TDL calibration work.

project.title: Loss Function Explorer
project.desc: Implement three loss functions from scratch. Visualize what each optimizes.
deliverables: Implement: MSE, Binary CE, Hinge loss (numpy only)
Plot loss vs prediction value for y=0 and y=1
Train logistic regression on 2D dataset with each loss
Compare: decision boundaries, probability calibration
README: when to choose each? Connect to your medical imaging work.
project.hint: numpy only — no PyTorch. Forces understanding of the math.

watch.title: CS229 Lecture 2 — Linear Regression and Gradient Descent
watch.focus: Full lecture. Cost function derivation, normal equation θ=(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy, why this matters for deep learning.

concept.title: The simplest model that teaches everything
concept.body: h_θ(x) = θᵀx. Cost: J(θ) = (1/2m)Σ(h-y)². Minimize by ∇J=0 → normal equation: θ=(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy. Every neural network layer IS a linear transformation + nonlinearity. Master this and you have the structure of every ML algorithm.
concept.analogy: Linear regression is the 'Hello World' of ML. It has everything: model, loss, optimization. Master it and you've mastered the structure of every ML algorithm that follows.
concept.visual:
h_θ(x) = θᵀx
J(θ) = (1/2m)·||Xθ-y||²
Normal eq: θ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy

When: n<10,000 features
Gradient descent: n large, iterative

challenge.q: X is 1000×500. What computational issue arises with normal equation and what is the alternative?

opts.t: XᵀX cannot be computed for n>500
(XᵀX)⁻¹ requires O(n³) inversion — slow for large n; use gradient descent
Normal equation only works for 2D
Requires normalized features

challenge.hint: Complexity of inverting a 500×500 matrix? What grows with more features?
challenge.exp: Matrix inversion is O(n³). n=500: 125M ops. n=10,000 (image pixels): 10¹² ops — infeasible. Gradient descent scales to millions of parameters because each step is O(mn). This is why neural networks use GD, not normal equation.

project.title: Linear Regression from Scratch
project.desc: Implement both normal equation and gradient descent.
deliverables: Normal equation: θ=(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy (numpy)
Gradient descent: θ=θ-α·(1/m)·Xᵀ(Xθ-y)
Apply both to regression dataset — verify same answer
Vary learning rate: show convergence vs divergence
Plot J vs iterations for different α values
README: why does GD scale to deep learning and normal equation does not?
project.hint: np.linalg.inv for normal equation. Manual loop for GD. Synthetic data: y=2x₁+3x₂+noise.

watch.title: CS229 Lecture 3 — Logistic Regression
watch.focus: Why linear fails for classification, sigmoid, log-likelihood derivation of BCE, decision boundary geometry.

concept.title: From regression to decisions
concept.body: For classification: pass linear output through sigmoid: σ(z)=1/(1+e⁻ᶻ). h_θ(x)=σ(θᵀx). Trained by maximizing log-likelihood (= minimizing BCE). Decision boundary: θᵀx=0. The final layer of ResNet/DenseNet IS logistic regression on learned features.
concept.analogy: Logistic regression: a linear model that outputs confidence. Sigmoid squishes any number into (0,1) — perfect for probability. A smooth threshold.
concept.visual:
σ(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})
P(y=1|x;θ) = σ(θᵀx)
Loss: -[y·log(σ)+(1-y)·log(1-σ)]
Decision boundary: θᵀx=0

challenge.q: Model outputs 0.48 for patient. Threshold=0.5. Patient has pneumonia. Is threshold choice ML or clinical?

opts.t: Pure ML — optimize threshold on validation with F1
Clinical decision — affects sensitivity/specificity tradeoff, must involve clinical judgment
Model is wrong — retrain
Threshold is always 0.5 for medical

challenge.hint: False negative (missed pneumonia) vs false positive (unnecessary treatment) have different clinical costs. Who decides?
challenge.exp: Clinical decision. 0.5 minimizes overall error, but in medicine, false negatives are usually far more costly. Radiologists decide the operating point. ML engineer provides model + PR curve. This IS trustworthy AI.

project.title: Pneumonia Classifier from Scratch
project.desc: Logistic regression for medical image classification. numpy only.
deliverables: Extract simple features from chest X-ray (pixel stats, HOG) — no CNN yet
Logistic regression: sigmoid, BCE, gradient descent (numpy)
Evaluate: accuracy, AUROC, F1
Precision-recall curve, clinical threshold at 0.9 sensitivity
README: explain sensitivity/specificity tradeoff. Who should choose the threshold?
project.hint: numpy only for model. sklearn only for evaluation metrics. PIL for image loading.

assignment.title: ML Foundations Audit
assignment.desc: Build a medical image classifier using only numpy, logistic regression, hand-crafted features.
deliverables: HOG features from chest X-rays (numpy/skimage)
Logistic regression with gradient descent (numpy, no sklearn)
Full evaluation: accuracy, AUROC, F1, precision-recall
Threshold analysis at 0.95 sensitivity
1-page report: data → features → model → loss → optimization → evaluation (for a medical student)
assignment.hint: Deliberate constraints: no PyTorch, no CNN. Forces understanding every step. The 1-page report is the main deliverable.
assignment.linkedin: Built a medical image classifier using only numpy. Forces you to understand every step: features, loss, gradient descent, evaluation. The constraints are the lesson. #MachineLearning #MedicalAI

watch.title: CS229 Lecture 2 (second half) + CS231N Lecture 7 (first 30 min)
watch.focus: Batch vs SGD intuition (CS229). Momentum, loss landscape, why vanilla GD fails at scale (CS231N).

concept.title: Moving downhill in parameter space
concept.body: Gradient descent: θ←θ-α·∇J(θ). Batch GD: all data, accurate but slow. SGD: one sample, noisy but fast. Mini-batch: practical compromise (32–256). Momentum: accumulate velocity — accelerates in consistent directions, dampens oscillations.
concept.analogy: Batch GD: plan perfect direction, take one big step. SGD: glance roughly downhill, quick step, repeat. Mini-batch: look at a handful of signs, take a reasonable step. Momentum: remember which way you've been rolling.
concept.visual:
SGD: θ ← θ - α·∇J(x⁽ⁱ⁾,θ)
Momentum: v ← βv+∇J, θ ← θ-α·v
β=0.9 (90% previous velocity)
Mini-batch: 32–256 samples per step

challenge.q: Training ResNet on chest X-rays. Loss oscillates wildly, α=0.1. Problem and fix?

opts.t: Momentum too high — set β=0
Learning rate too high — reduce α, try 0.001 or use LR finder
Batch size too small
SGD is wrong — use full batch GD

challenge.hint: Wild oscillation is the classic symptom of what hyperparameter being too large?
challenge.exp: α=0.1 is far too large for ResNet (typical: 1e-4 to 1e-2). Reduce by 10–100×. LR finder helps identify the right range.

project.title: Optimizer Comparison
project.desc: Compare SGD, SGD+Momentum, Adam on CNN training.
deliverables: Train same 3-layer CNN on CIFAR-10: SGD, SGD+momentum(β=0.9), Adam
Same LR and architecture for fair comparison
Plot: loss curves and val accuracy on same axes
Effect of different LRs for each optimizer
README: what does momentum add? Why does Adam usually converge faster?
project.hint: torch.optim.SGD(lr=0.01), SGD(lr=0.01,momentum=0.9), Adam(lr=0.001). Log loss every 10 batches.

secondary_watch.title: Deep Learning Specialization — Course 2: Practical Aspects of Deep Learning
secondary_watch.focus: Course 2 Week 1 (~3 hours). Focus on: regularization techniques, vanishing/exploding gradients, weight initialization, gradient checking. The most practical content in the specialization — bridges CS229 theory with what you actually implement. Free to audit.

watch.title: CS231N Lecture 7 — from 30 min: RMSprop, Adam
watch.focus: RMSprop intuition, Adam = momentum + RMSprop, adaptive LR per parameter. Why Adam is the default.

concept.title: One learning rate per parameter
concept.body: Adam: combines momentum (direction) with RMSprop (magnitude). Effective LR adapts per parameter. Large gradient parameters get smaller effective LR. AdamW: correct L2 regularization — standard for modern training.
concept.analogy: Adam is a smart GPS that adjusts speed per road — highway parameters get different speed than alley parameters. Each parameter has its own adaptive step size based on gradient history.
concept.visual:
Adam:
m_t = β₁·m_{t-1}+(1-β₁)·g_t  (momentum)
v_t = β₂·v_{t-1}+(1-β₂)·g_t² (variance)
θ_t = θ_{t-1}-α·m̂_t/(√v̂_t+ε)
Defaults: β₁=0.9, β₂=0.999, α=1e-3

challenge.q: Switch Adam → SGD+momentum for fine-tuning pretrained ResNet, same LR=0.001. Training unstable. Fix?

opts.t: Switch back to Adam — SGD cannot fine-tune pretrained models
Reduce LR significantly — SGD needs smaller LR than Adam for pretrained models
Increase batch size
Remove momentum for fine-tuning

challenge.hint: Adam has adaptive per-parameter LRs scaling down large gradients. SGD applies same LR to all. What does this mean for pretrained model gradient variance?
challenge.exp: In pretrained models, gradient magnitudes vary enormously between layers. SGD lr=0.001 causes large-gradient parameters to take huge steps. Reduce to 1e-4 or 1e-5.

project.title: LR Finder Implementation
project.desc: Implement the learning rate range test.
deliverables: LR range test: increase LR exponentially over 100 batches, log loss
Plot log(LR) vs loss — find the sweet spot (steepest descent)
Apply to Adam and SGD+momentum on medical classifier
Compare convergence and final accuracy with optimal LR
README: what LR for each optimizer? Why?
project.hint: Start at 1e-7, multiply by factor each batch. Optimal LR is steepest loss descent, left of the minimum.

watch.title: CS231N Lecture 7 second half — optimization landscape + BatchNorm
watch.focus: Why local minima are less problematic than saddle points. What BatchNorm does to the loss landscape.

concept.title: Why deep networks are hard to optimize
concept.body: Saddle points (zero gradient, not minimum) are far more common than local minima in high dimensions. BatchNorm: normalize to μ=0, σ=1, learn γ and β. Smooths loss landscape, allows higher LR. Always model.eval() at inference!
concept.analogy: A 2D loss landscape has clear valleys. A million-dimensional landscape mostly has saddle points — flat in most directions. BatchNorm flattens the terrain so all directions look similar — much easier to navigate.
concept.visual:
Saddle point: ∇J=0 but not minimum
In high dimensions: most critical points are saddles

BatchNorm: ẑ=(z-μ_B)/σ_B·γ+β
train: use batch stats
eval: use running stats
→ ALWAYS model.eval() before inference!

challenge.q: You add BatchNorm everywhere and forget model.eval(). What goes wrong during inference?

opts.t: Nothing — BatchNorm identical in train and eval
BatchNorm uses current batch stats instead of running stats — predictions inconsistent across batch sizes
Dropout activates incorrectly
Gradients computed unnecessarily

challenge.hint: Train mode: batch stats. Eval mode: running mean/var from training. What happens with batch_size=1?
challenge.exp: With batch_size=1 in train mode: mean=that single sample, var=0 → numerical instability. Even larger batches give inconsistent results. Common bug in medical imaging pipelines.

project.title: BatchNorm Effect Study
project.desc: Systematically study what BatchNorm does to training.
deliverables: Train same CNN: without BN, with BN after conv, with BN before activation
Compare: convergence speed, max stable LR, final accuracy
Visualize gradient magnitudes per layer with and without BN
Demonstrate: model.train() + batch_size=1 inference instability
README: explain in plain English why BN helps and what goes wrong without eval mode
project.hint: Log gradient norms: for name,p in model.named_parameters(): if p.grad: print(name, p.grad.norm()) after backward.

assignment.title: Training Pipeline Audit
assignment.desc: Rigorous training pipeline for medical classifier: LR finder, optimizer comparison, BatchNorm analysis.
deliverables: LR range test → optimal LR for your setup
Train: SGD+momentum, Adam, AdamW — compare convergence and final accuracy
BatchNorm ablation: with vs without, convergence curves
Gradient flow visualization: do gradients reach early layers?
README: justify every training decision as if writing the training section of a paper
assignment.hint: This is your training infrastructure. Once built well, reuse for every future experiment. Treat it like production code.
assignment.linkedin: Built rigorous ML training infrastructure: LR finder, optimizer benchmarking, BatchNorm ablation, gradient flow analysis. The foundation that makes research reproducible. #MLEngineering #DeepLearning

watch.title: CS229 Lecture 6 — Naive Bayes + probability review
watch.focus: Probability axioms, conditional probability, Bayes theorem, Gaussian distribution. Building blocks of your TDL section.

concept.title: Probability is the language of uncertainty
concept.body:
Key distributions: Bernoulli (binary), Gaussian N(μ,σ²) (appears everywhere via CLT), Categorical (multi-class). E[X] = Σx·P(x). Var[X] = E[X²]-E[X]².

Uncertainty decomposition, calibration, conformal prediction — all require fluent probability.
concept.analogy: Probability is the grammar of uncertainty. Without it, 'model outputs 0.87' means nothing. With it: 'I expect this correct in 87 of 100 similar cases' — and you can test whether that's true.
concept.visual:
Gaussian: P(x) = (1/√2πσ²)·exp(-(x-μ)²/2σ²)
E[X]=μ,  Var[X]=σ²
Bernoulli: P(X=1)=p, E[X]=p, Var[X]=p(1-p)

challenge.q: Model outputs P(pneumonia|x)=0.73. Radiologist asks: "what does 0.73 mean?" Correct answer?

opts.t: "Model is 73% accurate on cases like this"
"Among cases where model outputs ~0.73, approximately 73% should have pneumonia — if calibrated"
"Image is 73% similar to pneumonia training images"
"73% confidence means it is correct"

challenge.hint: A probability output is a statement about frequency. What frequency, under what assumption?
challenge.exp: Correct — with crucial condition "if calibrated." This is exactly what ECE measures and why calibration is clinically critical.

project.title: Probability Calibration Experiment
project.desc: Demonstrate what calibration means empirically.
deliverables: Train classifier, group test predictions into 10 confidence bins
For each bin: mean predicted confidence vs actual accuracy
Plot reliability diagram manually (not using a library)
Demonstrate artificially miscalibrated model (scale logits) vs calibrated
README: explain each point on the reliability diagram in plain language. Connect to TDL calibration work.
project.hint: Bin predictions: 0–0.1, 0.1–0.2, etc. Compute mean confidence and mean accuracy per bin. Plot vs diagonal.

watch.title: CS229 Lecture 5 — Generative Learning (first 30 min: MLE)
watch.focus: What MLE is, how log-likelihood leads to cross-entropy, why log is used, connection between MLE and standard loss functions.

concept.title: Your loss function is MLE in disguise
concept.body: MLE: find θ that maximizes P(data|θ). Gaussian model → minimizes MSE. Bernoulli → minimizes BCE. Every standard loss function has a probabilistic interpretation via MLE. Understanding this lets you design new loss functions consciously.
concept.analogy: MLE asks: 'which model parameters make the observed data most plausible?' It turns data into a question about model parameters.
concept.visual:
MLE: θ*=argmax_θ Σ log P(yⁱ|xⁱ;θ)
Bernoulli → binary CE loss
Gaussian → MSE loss
Multinomial → categorical CE

challenge.q: Predicting surgical instrument pose (angle, continuous). MSE or cross-entropy?

opts.t: Cross-entropy — always better for neural networks
MSE — assumes Gaussian noise around the true angle; appropriate for continuous regression
Hinge loss — standard for robotics
Dice loss — for localization tasks

challenge.hint: Continuous output → Gaussian likelihood → which loss? Binary → Bernoulli → which loss?
challenge.exp: MSE assumes Gaussian likelihood: minimizing MSE = maximizing Gaussian log-likelihood. For continuous angle prediction, this is correct. Cross-entropy is for discrete class labels.

project.title: Loss = Likelihood: Verify It
project.desc: Empirically verify that minimizing CE = maximizing log-likelihood.
deliverables: Implement: binary CE and its log-likelihood derivation — show equivalence
MSE and Gaussian log-likelihood — show equivalence
Train logistic regression minimizing CE vs maximizing log-likelihood — same result?
Plot: log-likelihood vs loss during training (should be mirror images)
README: what probabilistic model does binary CE assume? Connect to your medical classifier.
project.hint: L_CE = -[y·log(p)+(1-y)·log(1-p)]. Log-likelihood = Σ[y·log(p)+(1-y)·log(1-p)]. Negatives of each other.

watch.title: CS229 Lecture 7 — Bayesian intro (last 20 min)
watch.focus: Prior, likelihood, posterior. MAP estimation. Why regularization = prior. Foundation of TDL Bayesian section.

concept.title: Updating beliefs with evidence
concept.body: Bayes: P(θ|data) ∝ P(data|θ)·P(θ). MAP: find θ maximizing posterior. MAP + Gaussian prior = MLE + L2 regularization. Regularization = prior belief about parameters. Foundation of your TDL section.
concept.analogy: Before seeing X-rays, you believe most are normal (prior). After seeing a suspicious shadow (data), you update your belief (posterior). MAP finds the parameter setting that best combines prior + evidence.
concept.visual:
P(θ|D) ∝ P(D|θ)·P(θ)
MAP = argmax[log P(D|θ)+log P(θ)]
Gaussian prior → L2 regularization
Laplace prior → L1 regularization
Strong prior (high λ) = strong belief about weight size

challenge.q: ResNet-A: weight decay 1e-4 (L2 reg). ResNet-B: no regularization. What prior does ResNet-A assume?

opts.t: Laplace prior — L2 corresponds to Laplace
Gaussian prior N(0,σ²) — L2 regularization is MAP with Gaussian prior
Uniform prior — same as no regularization
Regularization has no Bayesian interpretation

challenge.hint: MAP with Gaussian prior: log P(θ) = -||θ||²/(2σ²). Compare to L2 penalty = λ·||θ||².
challenge.exp: L2 = MAP with Gaussian prior N(0,1/2λ). ResNet-B assumes uniform (flat) prior = MLE. This connection means you can reason about regularization choices as prior beliefs.

project.title: Prior Sensitivity & Regularization Study
project.desc: Empirically verify Bayesian interpretation of regularization.
deliverables: Train logistic regression: no reg, L2(λ=0.01), L2(λ=1.0), L1(λ=0.01)
Plot weight distributions — does Gaussian prior → Gaussian weights?
Implement MAP objective manually: log P(D|θ)+log P(θ) — verify = MLE+L2
Compare accuracy, weight magnitude, calibration
README: what prior belief does each regularization strength encode?
project.hint: Plot torch.cat([p.data.flatten() for p in model.parameters()]) as histogram for each setting.

assignment.title: Probabilistic ML System
assignment.desc: Build a probabilistic classifier: calibrated probabilities with explicit probabilistic foundations.
deliverables: Logistic regression via explicit MLE (log-likelihood maximization)
MAP training with Gaussian prior — show equivalence to weight decay
Calibrated probability output with reliability diagram
Bayesian model selection via BIC approximation
1-page report: every probabilistic choice — prior, likelihood, posterior approximation
assignment.hint: Connect to TDL section in the report. This assignment is the probabilistic foundation that makes MC Dropout and ensembles make sense.
assignment.linkedin: The math behind every DL loss function: MLE in disguise. Thread on how MLE connects to BCE, MSE, and why Bayesian thinking changes loss design. #MLFoundations #BayesianML

watch.title: CS229 Lecture 8 — Bias-Variance Tradeoff
watch.focus: Full lecture. One of the most important in CS229. Bias/variance definitions, model complexity effect, U-shaped test error curve.

concept.title: Why your model fails on new data
concept.body: Bias: error from wrong assumptions — too-simple model underfits. Variance: sensitivity to training data — too-complex model memorizes. Expected test error = Bias² + Variance + Irreducible noise. Reducing bias increases variance and vice versa.
concept.analogy: Bias: always aiming left of target regardless of how steady your hand is. Variance: your aim jumps randomly. Low bias + low variance = consistently hitting the target.
concept.visual:
Test error = Bias² + Variance + σ²_noise

Low complexity → high bias, low variance (underfit)
High complexity → low bias, high variance (overfit)
More data → reduces variance, NOT bias

challenge.q: ResNet-50: 99% train, 71% test. DenseNet-121: 94% train, 83% test. Same 500 chest X-ray dataset.

opts.t: ResNet-50 has lower bias and higher variance — overfitting; DenseNet-121 better regularized
DenseNet-121 has higher bias — cannot fit training data
Both underfitting
Dataset too small to conclude

challenge.hint: Which model has large train-test gap? Which has modest gap?
challenge.exp: ResNet-50: 28pt gap = high variance (overfitting). DenseNet-121: 11pt gap = better variance. Dense connections are a built-in regularizer — each layer accesses all previous features.

project.title: Bias-Variance Decomposition Experiment
project.desc: Empirically decompose bias and variance for different model complexities.
deliverables: Train increasing complexity models on small medical dataset
For each: compute bias² and variance across 10 bootstrap training runs
Plot: bias², variance, total error vs model complexity (U-curve)
Show: more data reduces variance — same model, different dataset sizes
README: sweet spot for your dataset? Architecture choice for small medical datasets?
project.hint: Bias² = (mean_predictions - truth)². Variance = variance of predictions across 10 bootstrap runs on held-out test set.

watch.title: CS231N Lecture 7 — regularization section (~40–60 min)
watch.focus: L2 intuition, dropout as regularization (training only, different from MC Dropout!), data augmentation as implicit regularization.

concept.title: Fighting variance without increasing bias
concept.body: L2: penalizes large weights. Dropout: random neuron zeroing during training — forces redundant representations. Different from MC Dropout (test-time uncertainty). Data augmentation: most effective regularizer for small medical datasets — but requires clinical validation.
concept.analogy: L2: hire a minimalist who avoids complexity. Dropout: remove random team members each day — the team learns not to rely on anyone. Augmentation: practice in many conditions so test day has no surprises.
concept.visual:
Dropout (training): zero each neuron with prob p
Test (standard): scale outputs by (1-p)
Test (MC Dropout): keep ON → uncertainty

Augmentation: same image, different appearance → same label

challenge.q: You apply horizontal flipping to chest X-rays. A radiologist says this is clinically wrong. Why?

opts.t: CNNs cannot learn from flipped images
Heart is left-sided normally — flipped X-ray shows it right-sided (situs inversus), a real clinical condition. Model learns wrong invariances.
Augmentation always hurts medical classifiers
Flipping breaks batch normalization

challenge.hint: What does a horizontally flipped chest X-ray look like clinically? Is left-right symmetry valid for chest anatomy?
challenge.exp: Cardiac anatomy is lateralized. Horizontal flip = situs inversus (rare real condition). If no situs inversus cases in dataset, flipping teaches a false invariance that could cause missing lateralization-based pathologies. Medical augmentation requires clinical validation.

project.title: Clinically Valid Augmentation Strategy
project.desc: Design and evaluate a clinically valid augmentation strategy for chest X-rays.
deliverables: Implement valid: random crop, small rotation (±5°), brightness/contrast, Gaussian noise
Implement invalid: horizontal flip, extreme rotation (negative examples)
Train with each, compare accuracy and test-set diversity
Visualize each augmented version — show to simulated radiologist
README: justify each augmentation clinically, as if for a medical AI journal
project.hint: albumentations. ShiftScaleRotate with small angles is safe. RandomBrightnessContrast simulates scanner variation.

watch.title: CS229 Lecture 8 second half — Model Selection and Cross-Validation
watch.focus: Why you need a separate test set, k-fold CV, danger of peeking at test data, holdout discipline.

concept.title: Measuring generalization honestly
concept.body: Train/val/test split: never use test for decisions. K-fold CV: rotate folds — more reliable estimates for small datasets. Data leakage: always split by PATIENT in medical imaging. Same patient in train and test inflates all metrics.
concept.analogy: Test set discipline: exam answers in a sealed envelope before the semester. Peeking while studying = meaningless exam score. Leakage = accidentally seeing the answers.
concept.visual:
Split by PATIENT, not by image:
❌ Wrong: random image split → patient A in train AND test
✓ Right: patient-level split → patient A ONLY in train

Leakage symptoms: AUROC >> real-world performance

challenge.q: Train on 80% of images, test on 20%. AUROC=0.94. Same patient in both sets. Real concern?

opts.t: Model memorized training images
Model learned patient-specific features (age, bone density) not pathology — AUROC is inflated
Split too small
AUROC is the wrong metric

challenge.hint: If same patient is in train and test, what patient-specific information might the model use?
challenge.exp: Patient-level leakage: model learns patient-specific features that help recognize the same patient in the test set. For truly new patients, performance will be much lower. Always split at patient level.

project.title: Evaluation Audit
project.desc: Audit your medical classifier for data leakage and evaluation bias.
deliverables: Check current split: any patient IDs shared between train/test?
Re-split by patient ID, re-evaluate — compare AUROC before/after
Implement k-fold CV (k=5) at patient level
Compare: image-level vs patient-level split AUROC (should drop)
README: what was the leakage? What does correct AUROC tell you about real-world performance?
project.hint: Group by patient ID before splitting. sklearn.model_selection.GroupKFold for patient-level CV.

assignment.title: Generalization Analysis Report
assignment.desc: Complete generalization analysis: bias-variance, regularization ablation, rigorous evaluation with patient-level splits.
deliverables: Bias-variance: training vs val curves across model sizes
Regularization ablation: no reg, dropout, weight decay, augmentation
Patient-level k-fold CV with leakage prevention
Final honest evaluation: mean ± std AUROC across folds
2-page report: "Generalization Analysis of [Your Model] for Chest X-ray Classification" — conference style
assignment.hint: Report: experimental setup, results table (mean±std across folds), discussion. This format appears in every paper you write.
assignment.linkedin: Rigorous ML evaluation: how to detect and fix data leakage in medical AI. Why patient-level CV gives a 20% more honest AUROC. Lessons from my own audit. #MedicalAI #MLEvaluation

watch.title: CS230 Lecture 1 — Introduction to Deep Learning (Andrew Ng)
watch.focus: Full lecture. What a neural network is, forward pass computation, why depth matters for hierarchical representations.

concept.title: Composing simple functions into powerful ones
concept.body: A neural network: f(x)=f_L(...f₂(f₁(x))). Without nonlinearities, depth adds nothing — collapses to linear. ReLU=max(0,z): no vanishing gradient for positive z. Sigmoid: squashes to (0,1), vanishing gradient. In practice: ReLU for hidden, sigmoid/softmax for output.
concept.analogy: Single neuron: one judge giving a vote. Neural network: committee of committees — lower committees analyze raw evidence, upper committees analyze lower committees' conclusions.
concept.visual:
ReLU: f(z) = max(0,z)  ← default hidden
Sigmoid: 1/(1+e^{-z})  ← binary output
Softmax: e^{z_i}/Σe^{z_j}  ← multi-class
Dead ReLU: z always<0 → gradient=0 → neuron dies

challenge.q: 30% of neurons in a deep ReLU network always output 0. Cause and fix?

opts.t: Network too deep — reduce to 3 layers
High LR + poor init → neurons permanently negative input, ReLU=0, gradient=0 forever
ReLU not for deep networks
Dead neurons are normal

challenge.hint: ReLU neuron dies when z is always ≤ 0. When does z become permanently negative?
challenge.exp: Dead ReLU: large negative gradient update (high LR) pushes weights to always produce z<0. Since ReLU gradient=0 for z≤0, weights never update — permanently dead. Fix: smaller LR, He initialization, or Leaky ReLU.

project.title: Neural Network from Scratch

units.title: Backpropagation
units.meta: Chain rule, gradient flow, vanishing gradients

watch.title: CS229 Lecture 9 — Backpropagation
watch.focus: Full lecture. Most important algorithm in deep learning. Chain rule, local gradients, efficient computation.

concept.title: Teaching the network by propagating blame
concept.body: Backprop: efficient ∂L/∂θ computation for all parameters via chain rule. δ_l = (W_{l+1}ᵀδ_{l+1})⊙f'(z_l). Vanishing gradients: if f'(z) is small (sigmoid in saturation), δ_l shrinks exponentially. Explains why ReLU replaced sigmoid and why skip connections help.
concept.analogy: Backprop is blame propagation. Final output wrong. Who is responsible? Last layer takes blame, passes proportional blame backward. Each layer's blame = how much it contributed.
concept.visual:
Chain rule: ∂L/∂W_l = δ_l · a_{l-1}ᵀ
δ_l = (W_{l+1}ᵀ δ_{l+1}) ⊙ σ'(z_l)
Vanishing: |σ'|<1 → δ_l→0 exponentially
ReLU: σ'=1 for z>0 → no vanishing (active neurons)

challenge.q: 10-layer sigmoid network. Gradient layer 1: 10⁻⁸. Layer 9: 10⁻². What is this?

opts.t: Exploding gradient — sigmoid amplifies
Vanishing gradient — sigmoid derivative max=0.25, multiplied 8 times ≈ 10⁻⁵ decay per layer
Dead neuron problem
Expected behavior

challenge.hint: σ'(z) ≤ 0.25. Multiply together 8 times. What happens?
challenge.exp: Vanishing gradient. 0.25⁸ ≈ 1.5×10⁻⁵. ReLU derivative = 1 for z>0 → gradients don't shrink through backprop. ResNet skip connections provide a direct gradient highway — explains their breakthrough.

watch.title: CS231N Lecture 9 — CNN Architectures (design section)
watch.focus: How to think about architecture design, width vs depth, bottleneck blocks, why skip connections changed everything.

concept.title: Architecture as a hypothesis about your problem
concept.body: Every architectural choice is a prior about problem structure. Depth: abstraction levels. Width: features per layer. Bottleneck: compress → conv → expand (same expressive power, 8× fewer parameters). For your work: ResNet-18 (quick experiments), DenseNet-121 (scarce medical data), EfficientNet (compute-constrained deployment).
concept.analogy: Architecture design is designing a factory. Depth = processing stations. Width = workers per station. Bottlenecks = compress materials for transport. Skip connections = express conveyor belts bypassing intermediate stations.
concept.visual:
ResNet bottleneck: 256→1×1(64)→3×3(64)→1×1(256)
Params: ~70K vs plain 3×3: ~590K (8.5× more)

EfficientNet: scale depth+width+resolution together
DenseNet: layer n receives features from ALL prior layers

challenge.q: 50ms latency constraint. ResNet-50: 45ms AUROC=0.91. ResNet-18: 12ms AUROC=0.87. EfficientNet-B0: 18ms AUROC=0.89. Which to deploy?

opts.t: ResNet-50 — highest accuracy always wins in medical AI
ResNet-18 — fastest and meets constraint
EfficientNet-B0 — best accuracy within the 50ms constraint
None — 50ms is too tight

challenge.hint: Which models meet <50ms? Among those, which has highest AUROC?
challenge.exp: EfficientNet-B0 meets constraint (18ms) and achieves highest AUROC (0.89) among compliant models. ResNet-50 could spike above 50ms. The 2% AUROC difference may be clinically significant.

watch.title: deeplearning.ai Course 2 — Week 1: Practical Aspects of Deep Learning
watch.focus: Normalizing inputs, weight initialization, vanishing/exploding gradients. ~2 hours, essential practical content.

concept.title: Starting right and staying stable
concept.body: He initialization: W~N(0,2/fan_in) for ReLU — keeps variance stable across layers. Too small → vanishing. Too large → exploding. BatchNorm: normalize to μ=0, σ=1, learn γ and β. LayerNorm: normalize per sample — used in Transformers/ViT.
concept.analogy: He init: right amount of fuel — not too little (stalls), not too much (floods). BatchNorm: automatic transmission — adjusts internally so you don't manually manage gradients through layers.
concept.visual:
He init: W~N(0, 2/fan_in) for ReLU
Xavier: W~N(0, 1/fan_in) for tanh/sigmoid
BatchNorm: ẑ=(z-μ_B)/σ_B·γ+β
LayerNorm: normalize per sample (not batch)

challenge.q: Initialize all weights to same constant W=0.01. 5 layers. Fundamental problem?

opts.t: Cannot learn — symmetry breaking fails when all weights identical
Small weights cause vanishing gradients
Requires different optimizer
Correct initialization for stable training

challenge.hint: If all weights identical, what do all neurons in the same layer compute? How does backprop update them?
challenge.exp: Symmetry breaking failure: all neurons compute the same output → same gradient → identical updates → effectively one neuron per layer. Cannot learn diverse features. Random init breaks symmetry.

watch.title: MIT 15.773 Hands-On Deep Learning — Practical DL session
watch.focus: Mixed precision training, gradient accumulation, model checkpointing, experiment tracking. Production skills.

concept.title: Training that actually finishes
concept.body: Mixed precision (FP16 forward + FP32 backward via GradScaler): 2× speed. Gradient accumulation: simulate large batch on small GPU. Checkpointing: save model+optimizer+epoch → resume interrupted training. Early stopping: stop when val loss plateaus.
concept.analogy: Mixed precision: rough calculator for most steps (fast), precise for final rounding (accurate). Gradient accumulation: save receipts across many batches before submitting expenses in one go.
concept.visual:
Mixed precision:
forward: FP16 → loss: FP32
GradScaler.scale(loss).backward()
GradScaler.step(optimizer)

Gradient accumulation:
loss = model(batch)/N; loss.backward()
if (i+1)%N==0: optimizer.step(); zero_grad()

Checkpoint every K epochs: save model weights + optimizer state + epoch number
More stable optimizer
Increase batch size

challenge.exp: Proper checkpointing: save {model_state_dict, optimizer_state_dict, epoch, val_loss, scheduler_state_dict} every K epochs. Keep best checkpoint separately. This is production infrastructure.

watch.title: UCLouvain — Modeling and Simulation of Multibody Systems Part I (edX, audit free)
watch.focus: Week 1-3: kinematics and dynamics of multibody systems. Focus on: how physical constraints translate into equations of motion, Newton-Euler dynamics, and the ROBOTRAN symbolic tool that generates Python code from your model. Directly applicable to your robot dynamics work.

concept.title: When physics meets learning
concept.body: Intelligent physical systems require both learning and dynamics. A robot arm has physical constraints that a neural network must respect. Physics-informed ML: incorporate known physical equations as loss terms. Sim-to-real transfer: train in simulation, deploy on real hardware.
concept.analogy: Standard ML: learn any function from data. Physics-informed ML: learn a function that also respects what we already know (Newton's laws, conservation, geometric constraints). Prior knowledge = less data needed.
concept.visual:
Physics-informed loss:
L = L_data + λ·L_physics
L_physics = ||NN(x) - f_physics(x)||²
f_physics = known differential equation
Result: model respects physical constraints

challenge.q: Neural network predicts robot arm end-effector position, one ignoring kinematics, one incorporating FK as a loss term. Same dataset. Which generalizes better to new joint configurations?

opts.t: Pure data-driven — more flexible, better generalization
Physics-informed — kinematics constraint prevents learning physically impossible configurations
Both generalize identically
Physics-informed overfits to kinematic model

challenge.hint: Kinematics equations are exact — they describe all valid configurations. What does adding this knowledge do to the function class?
challenge.exp: Physics-informed generalizes better. Kinematics constrains the function to physically valid configurations — the model cannot predict impossible arm positions. This reduces the effective function class, requiring less data.

units.title: Vectors, Matrices & Linear Transformations
units.meta: Geometry of data, column space, rank

watch.title: MIT 18.06 Linear Algebra — Lecture 1 (Gilbert Strang)
watch.focus: First 30 min. What a matrix does geometrically (transforms space), column space, why this matters for neural network layers.

concept.title: Every neural network layer is a linear transformation
concept.body: A matrix A transforms vectors: y = Ax. Geometrically: rotates, scales, projects. Every FC layer in your network IS matrix multiplication. Column space: all possible outputs of Ax. Rank: dimension of column space. Null space: lost information.
concept.analogy: A matrix is a machine that transforms space. Feed it a vector (a point in space), it outputs a new vector (the point transformed). Neural network layers are stacked transformation machines.
concept.visual:
y = Ax
A is n×m: maps R^m → R^n
Rank(A) = dim(column space) ≤ min(n,m)
Low-rank: bottleneck — information compression
Full-rank: no information loss

challenge.q: FC layer maps 512-dim input to 64-dim output (matrix A is 64×512). What does this say about information?

opts.t: No information lost — 512 dimensions preserved in 64 outputs
Information necessarily compressed — rank at most 64, from 512-dimensional input
Information increases — 64 outputs more efficient
Rank determines nothing about information

challenge.hint: Output is 64-dimensional. Can 64 numbers fully represent 512-dimensional input?
challenge.exp: Rank(A) ≤ 64. A 512-dim input is mapped to at most a 64-dim subspace — compression is forced. This is exactly what bottleneck layers do intentionally: compress to salient features, discard redundant ones.

watch.title: MIT 18.06 Lecture 21 — Eigenvalues + Lecture 29 — SVD
watch.focus: Eigenvalue meaning (directions that don't rotate), SVD decomposition, how PCA uses SVD.

concept.title: Finding the most important directions
concept.body: Eigenvalues/vectors: Av = λv. Directions that only scale under A. SVD: A = UΣVᵀ. Any matrix = rotation × scale × rotation. PCA: find directions of maximum variance (eigenvectors of covariance matrix). Project onto top-k directions → dimensionality reduction.
concept.analogy: Eigenvectors are the 'grain' of a transformation — directions along which it acts most cleanly. SVD finds the grain of any matrix. PCA finds the grain of your data.
concept.visual:
SVD: A = U·Σ·Vᵀ
U: output rotation
Σ: singular values (scale)
Vᵀ: input rotation

PCA: project onto top k columns of U
Variance explained = σᵢ²/Σσⱼ²

challenge.q: PCA on chest X-ray features. Top 50 principal components explain 89% of variance. What does this tell you?

opts.t: 89% of X-rays are normal
Feature space has strong structure — 50 directions capture most variation, rest is noise or redundancy
Use 100 components to be safe
PCA should not be used on image features

challenge.hint: Variance explained by k components = how much structure is captured in k dimensions.
challenge.exp: 89% variance in 50 components means strong feature space structure — most variation lies in 50 directions. The remaining 11% is likely noise. Enables compression: train classifier on 50 features instead of 512+ with minimal information loss.

watch.title: MIT 18.06 Lecture 9 — Independence, Basis, Dimension
watch.focus: Column space, linear independence, basis — and how these appear in attention mechanisms and gradient computation.

concept.title: Linear algebra as the language of deep learning
concept.body: Every DL operation is linear algebra: Self-attention: softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V — matrix multiplications. Gram matrix: XXᵀ — feature correlations. Gradient: ∂L/∂W = δ·aᵀ — outer product. Understanding in linear algebra terms lets you reason about complexity, parallelism, and numerical stability.
concept.analogy: Self-attention: 'how similar is each query to each key?' (dot product = similarity). Weight values by similarities. All matrix operations — linear algebra is the language.
concept.visual:
Self-attention:
Q,K,V = XW_Q, XW_K, XW_V
Attention = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)·V
Complexity: O(n²d) where n=sequence length

Gram: G = XXᵀ (n×n covariance)

challenge.q: ViT processes 196 patches (14×14 from 224×224). A medical video has 1000 frames as tokens. Computational challenge?

opts.t: No challenge — attention equally efficient for all lengths
Quadratic: 1000 tokens = 1M attention pairs vs 196²=38K. 26× more compute for 5× more tokens.
Attention cannot process more than 196 tokens
Only memory, not compute, scales with n

challenge.hint: O(n²): double the tokens → 4× the compute.
challenge.exp: 1000²=1M vs 196²=38K = 26× more attention pairs. This is why video transformers need efficient attention (linear attention, local attention) — standard self-attention is too expensive for long sequences like medical videos.
